newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda genocide survivors accuse returnees.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide survivors accuse returnees.

text.p: Francoise Mukakarisa, her eyes bulging in disbelief, shook hands with the men she says slaughtered her parents and neighbours in 1994 during Rwanda's genocide.
Although recovered from a rush of terrible memories and the deep fear their faces evoked, she can never forgive them.
Mukakarisa, a Tutsi housewife, bumped into the first man on Tuesday as she toured a squalid camp for hundreds of Hutu returnees in a schoolyard in the border town of Gisenyi.

"He just thrust out his hand and we held hands in the Rwandan way. He greeted me and I said something and tried to stop the pictures of my parents in my head," said Mukakarisa, 30, a normally cheerful, well-off mother of three from Gisenyi.
"I let go of his hand and tried to talk to other people. But I listened. He thought I couldn't hear him but he said to a friend: 'I regret coming back. Will she accuse me?,'" she said.
"That made me frightened. He knows exactly where we live."
On Wednesday, Mukakarisa returned to the camp and followed a Reuters journalist around, again greeting old Hutu friends sent to the school on their return from Zaire at the weekend.
Suddenly a stocky man in his mid-twenties wearing a T-shirt marked CARE International stepped out and grabbed her hand.
Mukakarisa's eyes again bulged out of her sockets as he said: "You look so well. I want to come round and visit you."
"Of course, come any time, you are welcome," she replied, before leaving as fast as possible without raising suspicion.
Asked how she could agree to his visit, Mukakarisa said: "It's not polite to refuse a request and he frightened me."

"I know both their names. My younger sister, who was 23, hid when they killed my parents on April 7, 1994 -- the second day of the genocide -- and saw the second one in a group of Interahamwe (Hutu militia) that went and killed the neighbours."

She said she wanted them to live forever in fear rather than be executed because the killing had to stop. "If they (the Rwandan government) want us to accuse them we will. If they say we have to keep quiet, we will have to," she added.

Three investigators for the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda's genocide arrived in Gisenyi on Tuesday, seeking evidence for the prosecution of Hutu leaders of the slaughter of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
They were denied entry into eastern Zaire from Gisenyi by rebel forces and headed back to Rwanda's capital on Wednesday.
Returnees who readily agreed to speak to Reuters at the school insisted all Interahamwe militiamen and former soldiers who took part in the genocide had fled deeper into Zaire.
But Gisenyi is buzzing with other sightings of suspected killers and some returnees say that members returned with them.

There are no guards of the Tutsi-dominated Rwanda army at the school and returnees can walk around town. They say authorities told them to stay there to be registered and until people occupying their homes move out. But some say they have already seen their homes are empty.
In the school outhouses crammed with returnees, several fit, young men leaning against a wall apart from the others refused to speak, glancing down when approached.
Mukakarisa survived the genocide as her house is near the border. The Interahamwe arrived in two cars on April 8, 1994.
"They burst in as we were having breakfast and said: 'Why weren't these killed yesterday.' Their eyes were red. They made me, my husband and the children sit as they looted the house.

"They kicked and slapped us and told us we would die later. Then they left but put two Interahamwe to guard the gate... Later our Hutu house boy went to see them and said they were drunk on beer and smoking drugs so we escaped," she said.

The family lived in the bush for a week until a Hutu woman took in the children. Another Hutu friend then bribed some Interahamwe guards and took them to a bar while Mukakarisa and her husband were smuggled across the border into eastern Zaire.

The Hutu house servant met them in the Zairean city of Goma when he and more than a million other Hutus fled in July 1994, but he later died of cholera. "We got the children when the woman looking after them also crossed," she said.

Mukakarisa then returned to Rwanda, while those she had fled were among the refugees in Zaire. She said when she met the man she believes killed her parents she thought of what her sister watched four years ago.

"My sister was hiding in the ceiling and saw before killing my mother they hacked off her legs. My father gave them 500,000 francs to save her life but they stole her necklace and chopped off her hands. Then they chopped my father's head right off.
"We never found the bodies. They took them away," she said. ($1=300 Rwandan francs)
